clue.text: A twopenny increase for rate

parts.note: taken as written
two pence, each written P
a raise is an increase, as in pay

explanation.surface: A small pay rise of two pence offered in return for a rate of work.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the standard abbreviation for a penny, so two of them make PP.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate something is to assess or judge its value, which is exactly what appraising does.

clue.text: Set apart old coin to subscribe

parts.note: the as was a Roman copper coin
to subscribe is to sign one's name at the foot of a document

explanation.surface: Putting aside an old coin to pay a subscription.
explanation.definitionFit: To assign something is to allot or earmark it for a particular purpose or person.

clue.text: Clear air as part of the service

parts.note: plain means clear, obvious
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A clear tune heard during a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainsong is unaccompanied chant sung in church liturgy, so it forms a section of worship.

clue.text: Speech from Downing Street, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a formal talk delivered to an audience
second meaning: a location where someone lives; Downing Street is home of the British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister gives a speech outside Number 10.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a speech made from the Prime Minister's residence, but the street itself is an example of the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is a formal speech, and also the street location where a person lives.

clue.text: Muslim divinity student frequently encountered in S Africa

indicators.note: a thing encountered in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the abbreviation for South Africa
oft is an old word for often

explanation.surface: An Islamic theology student often met in South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A softa is a student of Islamic law and theology attached to a mosque, especially in Turkey.

clue.text: Predicament I am found in throughout

parts.note: a pass is a difficult state of affairs, as in 'things have come to a pretty pass'
contracted to I'm

explanation.surface: Someone admits to being in a fix all the way through.
explanation.definitionFit: Passim is Latin used in footnotes to mean a reference occurs at many places all through a book.

clue.text: Hothead, in wrong situation, butts in here?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: astray means off course, in the wrong place
the head, the first letter, of hot

explanation.surface: A hothead in the wrong place pushes in where he isn't wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butts in' looks like interrupting; read it as cigarette butts going in.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashtray is a dish where smokers stub out cigarettes, so cigarette ends get put into it.

clue.text: Writer with large capacity for drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Gertrude ..., the American author
second meaning: a big earthenware beer mug

explanation.surface: An author who can hold a great deal of alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hard-drinking writer; 'large capacity for drink' is a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude Stein was a modernist author, and a stein is a large German beer mug holding plenty.

clue.text: For example, when I appeared instead of a note with a dash

definitions.text: For example, when I appeared instead of a

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
a dash is a short fast run

explanation.surface: Someone put the letter I where an A belonged in a musical note and a punctuation mark.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example: a typesetter printing I instead of A has made a typographical error.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a typing or printing error, such as one wrong letter set in place of another.

clue.text: To Micawber's credit, it was enough for a year's happiness

definitions.text: To Micawber's credit, it was enough for a year's happiness

parts.note: surface reading: praising a character for his contentment

parts.words: it was enough for a year's happiness
parts.note: setter's reading: the small surplus of income over spending in Mr Micawber's famous rule

explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's David Copperfield, Micawber says annual income twenty pounds, expenditure nineteen pounds nineteen and six, result happiness: the margin is half a shilling. 'Credit' is the accounting sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The old British coin worth six pennies is exactly the margin between Micawber's income and expenditure that he said brings happiness.

clue.text: Aloof manner in attitude of school head

parts.note: a stand is a position or attitude taken on an issue
taken as written
a school is a group of fish
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A haughty headteacher's cool demeanour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School head' reads as a headteacher, but the two words split: a school of fish, and head as a promontory, a ness as in Loch Ness or Sheerness.
explanation.definitionFit: Being distant and cold toward others, unfriendly reserve, is standoffishness.

clue.text: Herb's private article

parts.note: a gunner is the artillery equivalent of a private soldier
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A man named Herb owns some personal item.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb looks like a man's name owning something private; it is the definition, and private is a soldier's rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunnera is a huge-leaved perennial plant, and herb in the botanical sense covers any non-woody plant.

clue.text: Catch returning ringleader and accomplice

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the word for catch is read from its end

parts.note: to entrap is to catch
the leading letter of ring

explanation.surface: Police catch a gang's ringleader on his return, along with his accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringleader' reads as the gang boss; it is just the first letter of ring.
explanation.definitionFit: An accomplice is someone who acts jointly with another, a partner, especially in crime.

clue.text: MP. doctor, and poet, say

parts.note: first meaning: a member of the House of Commons, a man of the House
second meaning: a junior hospital doctor living in

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the name of the poet and listen to how it comes out

parts.note: A. E. Housman wrote A Shropshire Lad

explanation.surface: A list of three possible careers: politician, doctor and poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is A. E. Housman, whose name is spelt without the middle E but pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A houseman is a newly qualified British hospital doctor, and a House man is jokingly an MP, a member of Parliament's House.

clue.text: We have one, as a rule

definitions.text: We have one, as a rule

parts.note: surface reading: usually, generally speaking

parts.words: We have one, as a rule
parts.note: setter's reading: Britain possesses a form of government headed by a sovereign, which is a kind of rule

explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' reads as 'usually'; here it means 'as our system of rule', since Britain has a king or queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A system of government with a hereditary sovereign as head of state is a type of rule Britain has.

clue.text: Join the old folk in the country

indicators.note: join tells us to put the following two parts side by side

parts.note: ye is an archaic spelling of the
men are people, folk

explanation.surface: An invitation to come and live with elderly people out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' suggests the countryside; here it means a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Yemen is a nation in the south of the Arabian peninsula.

clue.text: Maiden's providing cause for concern

parts.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over
the contraction expanded
giving is a synonym of providing

explanation.surface: A young woman's behaviour is worrying people.
explanation.walkthrough: Maiden suggests a young woman; in cricket a maiden is an over with no runs scored, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: A misgiving is a feeling of doubt or apprehension, a worry or concern about something.

clue.text: Metal tin a lump, possibly

indicators.note: possibly hints that the words may be one possible arrangement of other letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Tin, a metal, might come in a lump.
explanation.walkthrough: Tin looks like the metal being defined, but it is only fodder; the defined metal is another.
explanation.definitionFit: Platinum is a precious silvery-white metallic element used in jewellery and catalysts.

clue.text: Run a serious sort of theatre

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for running away
second meaning: short for legitimate theatre, straight drama as opposed to musicals or variety

explanation.surface: An instruction to manage a playhouse devoted to serious drama.
explanation.walkthrough: Run looks like managing the theatre; it is the slang verb to leg it, meaning flee.
explanation.definitionFit: Legit is showbusiness slang for legitimate drama, conventional stage plays, and leg it is British slang for run off.

clue.text: Not like novel he wrote

indicators.note: novel means new and unusual, so these letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A disclaimer that some book is unlike the one the author wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel looks like a book he wrote; it is the anagram signal, and the definition is the writer himself.
explanation.definitionFit: J. R. R. Tolkien was the author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, a man who wrote.

clue.text: To try the patience of saints is gratuitous

parts.note: to needle someone is to irritate them
S is the abbreviation for saint, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Annoying even the holiest people is quite uncalled for.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gratuitous is uncalled for and unnecessary, done without good reason.

clue.text: Pupil given pound for work?

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra
someone paid for work is an earner

explanation.surface: A schoolchild receives a pound for doing chores.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'for work' is a loose description: one who is paid for work is an earner.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil is someone being taught, a student or learner.

clue.text: Northern port accessible in October, generally

indicators.note: something accessible in a place can be found there, so the letters sit within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the start of the next

explanation.surface: A northern harbour that can usually be reached in autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: Bergen is a major seaport on the west coast of Norway, in northern Europe.

clue.text: Jill fetching water in glass

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in the nursery rhyme Jack fell down and Jill came tumbling after
second meaning: a flat-bottomed drinking vessel

explanation.surface: Jill from the nursery rhyme carrying water in a drinking glass.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Jack and Jill' the pair go up the hill to fetch a pail of water, and Jill tumbles down after Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: Jill is one who tumbles, and a tumbler is also a straight-sided drinking vessel without stem.

clue.text: Make fast time in this?

indicators.note: in tells us the time letter is placed inside the word for make fast

parts.note: to moor a boat is to make it fast, tie it up
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A question about where you might go quickly against the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make fast time' reads as hurrying; split it, and make fast is to tie up a boat. The whole clue then also describes a car, a vehicle for quick journeys.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor is an informal British word for a car, the vehicle in which one could travel quickly.

clue.text: Confection of plainer sort

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version, so these letters are rearranged into another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sweet that is less fancy than usual.
explanation.definitionFit: Praline is a sweet made from nuts cooked in boiling sugar, a type of confectionery.

clue.text: Artistic infants set it up

parts.note: to set something is to put it down

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Children with a creative streak arrange something.
explanation.definitionFit: Putti are chubby naked cherub figures in Renaissance and Baroque paintings and sculpture.

clue.text: Lacking rank, however

parts.note: not with means without, lacking
standing is status or rank

explanation.surface: Someone without social status, nevertheless.
explanation.definitionFit: Notwithstanding and however both work as adverbs meaning nevertheless, in spite of that.

clue.text: Damage in a mooring area

parts.note: to mar is to damage
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boat gets damaged while tied up in a mooring area.
explanation.definitionFit: A marina is a purpose-built harbour where yachts and pleasure boats tie up.

clue.text: One element or another turned with information

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so the two short words before it are read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
a different element, the metal tin
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A chemistry question: one element or another rotated, with some data attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' means another element, picking up the definition's word: tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrogen is a chemical element, the colourless gas making up most of the air.
